newsitem.title: USA: Eastwood to pay ex-lover in settlement of her suit.
newsitem.headline: Eastwood to pay ex-lover in settlement of her suit.

text.p: Clint Eastwood agreed on Tuesday to pay his ex-lover Sondra Locke an undisclosed sum to settle a civil suit in which she claimed the movie star sabotaged her screen career.

The settlement was disclosed minutes before a jury was to resume deliberating. Jurors who were dismissed by the judge after the settlement was announced later told Reuters they had been ready to find in favour of Locke, who was seeking $2.5 million from Eastwood.

Juror Robert Campbell said the panel had agreed by a 10-2 vote in its first day of deliberations on Friday to find for Locke, who lived with Eastwood for 13 years. "We all agreed she should have gotten something, it was just how much," he said, adding that jurors suggested damages ranging from $15,000 to $10 million.

Neither Locke nor Eastwood was in court on Tuesday, and their lawyers declined to say how much Eastwood had agreed to pay his former lover. But Eastwood lawyer Raymond Fisher told reporters the actor-director was pleased with the agreement, which he called "a mutually agreeable settlement" that would allow both to get "moving on with their lives."
"I feel like some giant albatross in my life has gone away," Locke told a news conference later, saying the case was "never about money."
"I really can't describe what it meant to me to have the opportunity to say what had happened to me," she said.
Asked if she was still friends with Eastwood, she replied, "I definitely wouldn't say that's the case."

Locke's lawyer, Peggy Garrity, said the settlement was a straight cash payment and involved no future deals. "This settlement ends the litigation between Sondra Locke and Clint Eastwood, we hope, forever."
Locke, an actress who met Eastwood on the set of "The Outlaw Josey Wales" in 1975, originally filed a "palimony" suit in 1989, claiming assets the couple accumulated during their relationship.

She dropped that suit when Eastwood agreed to secure her a director's contract worth $1.5 million at Warner Bros. But she contended later the contract was a sham, because Eastwood had a secret deal with the studio to reimburse it for losses incurred by any Locke film, thus destroying any credibility she had in Hollywood.
"I was tricked. I wasn't told (about the indemnity deal), and I had a right to know," Locke said in testimony last week.

Eastwood claimed he made the deal to help Locke's career, but at least one juror thought Eastwood calculated that reimbursing Warner Bros. for any potential losses would be cheaper than a palimony settlement with Locke.
"Clint Eastwood did whatever was necessary to get out of his palimony suit. ... He stood to lose a lot," juror Brenda Williams said.

Locke's previous directorial efforts, "Ratboy" and "Impulse," were not commercial successes, and in three years under the Warner Bros. contract, none of her 30 suggested projects was ever developed into a film.

Juror Campbell told Reuters the panel did not believe testimony from Warner Bros. executives that Locke was treated no differently from any other director. "We didn't buy any of their stories. We thought it was a conspiracy," he said. "It seemed that Clint Eastwood had so much influence in Hollywood ... that he knew they would do anything not to upset him."
Referring to the "so-called deal" with Warner Bros., juror Williams said no jurors believed Eastwood, who said he had secured Locke's contract to help her career.

"It really wasn't worth the paper it was written on. Maybe she's not a good producer. Maybe she's not a good director. But give her the facts. Give her the opportunity to get out there and try," Williams said.
